title: Alvarez II.9: God premoves free choice to the act of sin as act and being; the malice is from the deficient will
source_text: XXI. Caput vero nonum hunc titulum praefert. Quod Deus praevia motione liberum arbitrium vere efficienter, sive ad modum causae Physicae, praemoveat ad actum peccati, in quantum actus, & ut ens est. Ipsum vero caput incipit his verbis, Quae dicta sunt de praedeterminatione Voluntatis ad actus bonos, extendi debent ad actum peccati, in quantum actus & ens est. Unde quicquid entitatis reperitur in quocunque actu peccati, etiamsi alias sit intrinsece malus, debet reduci in Deum, tanquam in primam causam praemoventem, & praedeterminantem actuali motione Voluntatem creatam ad talem actum, in quantum actus est, & secundum quod est ens. Postea vero ostensurus quomodo ex eo quod Deus est causa prima praemovens, & praedeterminans voluntatem creatam ad actum intrinsece malum, exempli gratia ad actum blasphemiae, aut odii in Deum, non sequitur Deum esse causam malitiae moralis quae talibus actibus inest, dicit deformitatem peccati, seu malitiam moralem non sequi intrinsece, & ex natura rei ad actum blasphemiae, vel odii Dei, secundum suam essentiam, ut actus est; neque ut est ens in genere naturae, etiam in individuo; sed ut procedit a voluntate creata deficiente; & ideo in voluntatem deficientem, & non in Deum, debere refundi malitiam moralem, & defectum peccati.
pass_a_gloss: But the ninth Chapter bears this title. That God by previous motion truly efficiently, or after the manner of a Physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin, in so far as it is an act, and as it is a being. But the chapter itself begins with these words, What has been said of the predetermination of the Will to good acts, ought to be extended to the act of sin, in so far as it is an act and a being. Whence whatever of entity is found in any act of sin whatever, even if otherwise it be intrinsically evil, ought to be reduced to God, as to the first cause premoving, and predetermining by actual motion the created Will to such an act, in so far as it is an act, and according as it is a being. But afterwards being about to show how from this that God is the first cause premoving, and predetermining the created will to an act intrinsically evil, for example to an act of blasphemy, or of hatred against God, it does not follow that God is the cause of the moral malice which is in such acts, he says that the deformity of sin, or moral malice does not follow intrinsically, and from the nature of the thing upon the act of blasphemy, or of hatred of God, according to its essence, as it is an act; nor as it is a being in the genus of nature, even in the individual; but as it proceeds from a deficient created will; and therefore the moral malice, and the defect of sin, ought to be poured back upon the deficient will, and not upon God.
pass_b_english: The heading of chapter 9 reads: 'That God, by a prior motion, truly as an efficient cause or in the manner of a physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.'

The chapter opens: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. Hence whatever being is found in any act of sin, even one otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause who premoves and, by an actual motion, predetermines the created will to that act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

Then, to show why it does not follow from God's being the first cause who premoves and predetermines the created will to an intrinsically evil act, such as blasphemy or hatred of God, that God causes the moral malice in such acts, he says this: the deformity of sin, or moral malice, does not follow intrinsically and by the nature of the case from the act of blasphemy or hatred of God in its essence as an act, nor as a being in the order of nature, even taken individually. It follows from the act as it comes from a created will that fails. The moral malice and the defect of sin must therefore be laid on the failing will, not on God.

lemmas.latin: in quantum actus, & ut ens est
lemmas.gloss: in so far as it is an act, and as it is a being

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
